overview: A Window specification defines how rows are grouped (partitionBy), ordered (orderBy), and framed (rowsBetween/rangeBetween) for window functions, which compute a value for each row based on a set of related rows without collapsing them.
Unlike groupBy, which reduces each group to one aggregated row, a window function returns one output row per input row, attaching the aggregate or ranking computed over its window.

The frame (rowsBetween vs. rangeBetween, with bounds unboundedPreceding, currentRow, unboundedFollowing) controls exactly which rows within a partition feed each calculation, enabling running totals, moving averages, rankings, and lag/lead comparisons.
learningObjectives: Build a Window spec with Window.partitionBy and Window.orderBy and apply window functions over it.
Distinguish window functions from groupBy aggregations and explain why windows preserve row count.
Define frames correctly using rowsBetween vs. rangeBetween with unboundedPreceding/currentRow/unboundedFollowing, and know the default frame behavior.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A window specification (pyspark.sql.Window) is an immutable object describing a partitioning (partitionBy), an ordering (orderBy), and a frame (rowsBetween or rangeBetween with boundary markers). A window function evaluated WITH that spec computes, for every input row, an aggregate, ranking, or analytic value over the frame of rows defined relative to that row within its partition, returning the same number of rows as the input.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: A window lets each row 'look around' at related rows and compute something, while still staying its own row. partitionBy decides which rows are in the same neighborhood (e.g., all sales for the same store), orderBy decides their order within the neighborhood (e.g., by date), and the frame decides how far each row can look (e.g., all earlier rows up to now, for a running total). groupBy would squash each neighborhood into one summary row; a window keeps every row and just adds the answer alongside it.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Window (analytic) functions are part of the SQL:2003 standard and long existed in databases like Oracle and PostgreSQL. Spark added them to the DataFrame API and Spark SQL in version 1.4 (2015) via the pyspark.sql.Window class, bringing partition/order/frame-based analytics such as ranking and running aggregates to distributed datasets, with Catalyst handling the shuffle-and-sort needed to evaluate each partition.

whyItMatters.business: Running totals, moving averages, rankings (top-N per category), period-over-period comparisons, and deduplication are everyday analytics needs that window functions express directly, powering dashboards and reports.
whyItMatters.engineering: Windows replace fragile self-joins and manual loops with a single declarative spec, making analytic logic concise, correct, and optimizable.
whyItMatters.scalability: Catalyst evaluates windows by shuffling on the partition key and sorting within partitions; choosing good partition keys keeps this scalable, while a missing partitionBy forces all data into one partition.
whyItMatters.cost: Well-partitioned windows avoid the expensive O(n^2) self-joins teams otherwise write, reducing shuffle and compute cost.
whyItMatters.reliability: Explicit frames give deterministic, well-defined results (e.g., correct running totals), whereas relying on default frames or unordered windows can produce surprising or nondeterministic output.

coreComponents.name: Window.partitionBy
coreComponents.definition: Divides the rows into independent partitions (groups) over which the window function is computed separately.
coreComponents.purpose: To scope the calculation to related rows (e.g., per customer, per store) so each row's window only sees its own group.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Triggers a shuffle on the partition key; if omitted, all rows fall into a single partition (computed on one task, a common performance trap).

coreComponents.name: Window.orderBy
coreComponents.definition: Defines the ordering of rows within each partition, which determines sequence-dependent results and the default frame.
coreComponents.purpose: To give meaning to row order for ranking and running calculations (e.g., order sales by date).
coreComponents.responsibilities: Sorts rows within each partition; required for ranking functions (row_number, rank) and for range/row frames to be meaningful.

coreComponents.name: Frame (rowsBetween / rangeBetween)
coreComponents.definition: Specifies which rows within the ordered partition are included in each row's calculation, using boundaries unboundedPreceding, currentRow, unboundedFollowing, or numeric offsets.
coreComponents.purpose: To control the exact set of rows feeding the aggregate (e.g., all prior rows for a running total, or a sliding window for a moving average).
coreComponents.responsibilities: rowsBetween counts physical rows by position; rangeBetween includes rows whose ORDER BY value falls within a value range relative to the current row.

internalWorking: Spark shuffles the DataFrame so all rows sharing the partitionBy key land on the same executor partition (no partitionBy means a single global partition).
Within each partition, rows are sorted according to orderBy so sequence-dependent functions and frames are well-defined.
For each row, Spark materializes the frame (the subset of rows defined by rowsBetween/rangeBetween) and applies the window function (sum, avg, row_number, lag, etc.) over that frame.
The computed value is attached to the row; row count is unchanged, unlike groupBy which emits one row per group.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: DataFrame -> shuffle on partitionBy key -> sort within partition by orderBy -> for each row build frame (rowsBetween/rangeBetween) -> apply window function -> output (same row count, new column)
dataFlowWalkthrough: 2. Spark shuffles sales so each store's rows are co-located, then sorts them by sale_date.
3. For each row, the frame is all rows from the first sale up to the current row; F.sum('amount').over(w) sums them into a running total.
4. Every original sale row is returned with an added running_total column; no rows are collapsed.

keyTerminology.meaning: A function (aggregate, ranking, or analytic) evaluated over a window frame that returns one value per input row.
keyTerminology.importance: It is the mechanism that lets you compute group-relative values without losing row-level detail.

keyTerminology.meaning: The subset of rows within a partition, defined by rowsBetween or rangeBetween, that a window function operates on for a given row.
keyTerminology.importance: Controls exactly which rows are aggregated, distinguishing a running total from a moving average or a full-partition aggregate.

keyTerminology.meaning: A physical-offset frame counting a fixed number of rows before/after the current row (e.g., 2 preceding to current).
keyTerminology.importance: Gives deterministic, position-based windows regardless of the ORDER BY values, ideal for fixed-size moving windows.

keyTerminology.meaning: A logical-value frame including all rows whose ORDER BY value lies within a range relative to the current row's value.
keyTerminology.importance: Groups rows by value proximity (e.g., all rows within 7 days), and treats rows with equal ORDER BY values (peers/ties) together.

keyTerminology.meaning: Frame boundary markers: the first row of the partition, the current row, and the last row of the partition respectively.
keyTerminology.importance: These define open-ended frames such as 'everything up to now' (running total) or 'everything from now on'.

importantConcepts.explanation: groupBy collapses each group into a single aggregated row, losing detail. A window function computes the same kind of aggregate but returns one row per input row, attaching the group-level value to every detail row, so you keep granularity and the aggregate together.

rowsBetween counts physical rows by position (e.g., the 3 rows ending at the current row). rangeBetween selects rows by the ORDER BY value range (e.g., all rows within 7 days of the current row's date) and includes all tied/peer rows with the same ordering value, which rowsBetween does not.

If you specify orderBy but no explicit frame, the default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (a running aggregate that includes ties). With no orderBy and no frame, the default is the entire partition (ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING). This default with ties is a frequent source of surprising results.

variationsAndTypes: **Ranking functions:** row_number, rank, dense_rank, ntile, percent_rank (require orderBy).
**Aggregate window functions:** sum, avg, min, max, count over a frame (running or sliding totals).
**Analytic functions:** lag, lead (access prior/next row values), first, last, nth_value.
**Frame types:** rowsBetween (physical offsets) vs. rangeBetween (value range).
**Boundaries:** unboundedPreceding, currentRow, unboundedFollowing, and numeric offsets (e.g., -2, 0, 3).
advantages: **Preserves row-level detail** while adding group-relative metrics.
**Declarative and concise:** replaces self-joins and manual loops with one spec.
**Versatile:** running totals, moving averages, rankings, top-N, deduplication, and period comparisons.
**Optimizable:** Catalyst handles the shuffle/sort and can combine compatible window functions over the same spec.
disadvantages: **Shuffle cost:** partitionBy triggers a shuffle, and skewed partition keys cause stragglers.
**Single-partition trap:** omitting partitionBy forces all data onto one task, which can OOM or be very slow.
**Frame subtlety:** default-frame and rangeBetween tie semantics surprise users and cause subtle bugs.
**Ordering required:** many functions are meaningless or nondeterministic without orderBy.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use windows when you need a per-row result that depends on related rows: running totals, moving averages, rankings within a group, top-N per category, lag/lead comparisons, or deduplication by row_number.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid windows when a plain groupBy aggregation (one row per group) suffices, since groupBy is cheaper; also avoid windows without partitionBy on large data, as everything funnels into one partition.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Imagine students lined up by exam date within each classroom. partitionBy is the classroom (each room ranked separately). orderBy is the line order (by date). The frame is how far each student can see: 'everyone ahead of you up to your spot' (unboundedPreceding to currentRow) gives a running class average as the line progresses. groupBy, by contrast, would just announce the single class average and send everyone home, keeping no individual.

commonMisconceptions.reality: rowsBetween counts physical rows by position; rangeBetween selects rows by ORDER BY value and groups all tied/peer rows together. With duplicate ordering values they give different results.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Adding orderBy to a window without a frame just sorts the rows.
commonMisconceptions.reality: orderBy without an explicit frame changes the default frame to RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW (a running aggregate including ties), so a sum 'over' that window becomes a running total, not a full-partition total.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Window evaluation requires a shuffle on the partitionBy key and a sort within partitions; choose a partition key with good cardinality and low skew, and use AQE skew handling to avoid straggler tasks.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Always specify orderBy for sequence-dependent functions and an explicit frame to make results deterministic; ties in orderBy can otherwise make row_number/first/last nondeterministic.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Window stages recover via Spark's lineage like any shuffle stage; large per-partition frames increase memory pressure and risk spill or OOM on skewed partitions.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Watch the Spark UI for the Window stage's shuffle size and for skewed task durations indicating an uneven partition key.
productionConsiderations.security: No special security concerns beyond standard data access; ensure partition keys do not inadvertently expose sensitive groupings in outputs.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Combine multiple window functions sharing the same spec so Catalyst computes them in one window operator; avoid unnecessary windows where groupBy suffices.
productionConsiderations.performance: Pre-filter and pre-aggregate before windowing to shrink data; avoid omitting partitionBy on large datasets; prefer rowsBetween over rangeBetween for large frames when peer semantics are not needed, as range frames can be costlier.

codeExamples.title: partitionBy + orderBy: ranking and row_number
codeExamples.overview: Rank sales within each store by amount and pick the top sale per store using row_number over a partitioned, ordered window.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()

sales = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("A", "2026-06-01", 100), ("A", "2026-06-02", 250), ("A", "2026-06-03", 250),
     ("B", "2026-06-01", 75), ("B", "2026-06-02", 300)],
    ["store_id", "sale_date", "amount"],
)

# Window: partition by store, order by amount descending
w = Window.partitionBy("store_id").orderBy(F.col("amount").desc())

ranked = (
    sales
    .withColumn("row_num", F.row_number().over(w))   # unique 1..n, breaks ties arbitrarily
    .withColumn("rnk", F.rank().over(w))             # ties share rank, leaves gaps
    .withColumn("dense_rnk", F.dense_rank().over(w)) # ties share rank, no gaps
)

# Top sale per store
top_per_store = ranked.filter(F.col("row_num") == 1)
ranked.show()
top_per_store.show()
codeExamples.breakdown: The window partitions by store_id and orders by amount descending. row_number assigns a unique sequence per store (arbitrarily breaking the 250/250 tie in store A), rank gives tied rows the same rank with a gap after, and dense_rank gives the same rank with no gap. Filtering row_num == 1 yields the top sale per store.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Each row gets row_num, rnk, and dense_rnk within its store; top_per_store shows store A's 250 sale (one of the ties) and store B's 300 sale.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Without orderBy, ranking functions error or are meaningless. row_number breaks ties nondeterministically unless you add tiebreaker columns to orderBy.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Add a deterministic tiebreaker (e.g., .orderBy(F.col('amount').desc(), 'sale_date')) so row_number is reproducible across runs.

codeExamples.title: Running total vs. moving average: frames with rowsBetween
codeExamples.overview: Compute a running total (unboundedPreceding to currentRow) and a 3-row moving average using explicit rowsBetween frames.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

# Order by date within each store
base = Window.partitionBy("store_id").orderBy("sale_date")

# Running total: from first row up to current row
running_frame = base.rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)

# Moving average: current row plus the 2 preceding rows (3-row window)
moving_frame = base.rowsBetween(-2, Window.currentRow)

result = (
    sales
    .withColumn("running_total", F.sum("amount").over(running_frame))
    .withColumn("moving_avg_3", F.avg("amount").over(moving_frame))
)

result.orderBy("store_id", "sale_date").show()
codeExamples.breakdown: Both windows share partitionBy('store_id').orderBy('sale_date'). The running_total frame spans every row from the partition start to the current row. The moving_avg_3 frame spans the current row and the two physically preceding rows (offset -2 to 0), giving a fixed 3-row sliding average regardless of date gaps.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Each store's rows show a cumulative running_total growing down the partition and a moving_avg_3 averaging the current and two prior amounts.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Confusing rowsBetween offsets (-2 means two rows back, not two days back). Forgetting that the default frame (orderBy, no rowsBetween) already gives a running total, so an explicit frame here is for clarity and for the moving average.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Define the base window once and derive frames from it; Catalyst can evaluate multiple window functions over compatible specs efficiently.

codeExamples.title: rowsBetween vs. rangeBetween and the default frame
codeExamples.overview: Contrast a physical-row frame with a value-range frame on data with ties, and show the default frame behavior.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

base = Window.partitionBy("store_id").orderBy("amount")

# Physical: current row and the single preceding row
rows_frame = base.rowsBetween(-1, Window.currentRow)
# Logical: rows whose amount is within [current_amount - 0, current_amount] i.e. all ties at current value and below by 0
range_frame = base.rangeBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)

cmp = (
    sales
    .withColumn("sum_rows", F.sum("amount").over(rows_frame))
    .withColumn("sum_range", F.sum("amount").over(range_frame))
    # Default frame: orderBy present, no explicit frame => RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW
    .withColumn("sum_default", F.sum("amount").over(base))
)

cmp.orderBy("store_id", "amount").show()
codeExamples.breakdown: rows_frame sums the current row plus exactly one physically preceding row. range_frame sums all rows from the partition start whose amount is <= the current amount, and crucially includes ALL tied rows at the current amount together. sum_default uses no explicit frame, so Spark applies the default RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW, identical to range_frame here, demonstrating the default running-aggregate-with-ties behavior.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: For store A's two rows tied at amount 250, sum_range and sum_default include both 250s at that boundary (so both tied rows show the same cumulative value), while sum_rows only adds one preceding physical row, producing different numbers.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Expecting rangeBetween to behave like rowsBetween on ties; the default frame silently being RANGE (not ROWS) when orderBy is set surprises people doing 'total per partition'.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: If you want a true per-partition total ignoring order, use Window.partitionBy(...) with NO orderBy (default frame becomes the whole partition), or set rowsBetween(unboundedPreceding, unboundedFollowing) explicitly.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A retailer needs, per store, a daily running revenue total, a 7-day moving average, the rank of each day's sales within the store, and deduplicated records keeping only the latest entry per (store, day), all without losing the per-day detail.
endToEndExample.inputData: Daily sales: store_id, sale_date, amount, ingest_ts (used to pick the latest duplicate).
endToEndExample.architecture: A Spark job reads the sales table, defines reusable Window specs (partitioned by store, ordered by date), applies running/sliding aggregates and ranking, deduplicates with row_number, and writes the enriched table partitioned by store.
endToEndExample.output: An enriched, deduplicated sales table where each surviving day row carries running_total, moving_avg_7, and day_rank for its store.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Inspect the Window stage shuffle size and task-time distribution in the Spark UI; alert on skew where a few large stores dominate runtime.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Add deterministic tiebreakers to every ranking orderBy to avoid nondeterministic dedup; validate that row counts after dedup are <= input and that running totals are monotonic non-decreasing for non-negative amounts.
endToEndExample.finalResult: A reliable analytics table delivering running totals, moving averages, rankings, and clean deduplication in one pass, replacing fragile self-joins with concise, optimizable window specs.

industryUseCases.problem: Computing per-customer running purchase totals and ranking products within each category for recommendations.
industryUseCases.solution: Window.partitionBy(customer/category).orderBy(...) with running-sum frames and rank/dense_rank to keep per-row detail alongside group metrics.
industryUseCases.benefits: Single-pass analytics without self-joins, preserving line-item detail while attaching running totals and top-N rankings.

industryUseCases.problem: Calculating moving averages and period-over-period changes of stock metrics per symbol.
industryUseCases.solution: Partition by symbol, order by timestamp, and use rowsBetween sliding frames plus lag/lead to compute moving averages and deltas.
industryUseCases.benefits: Accurate, deterministic time-series indicators computed at scale with declarative frames instead of manual ordering logic.

industryUseCases.problem: Deduplicating event streams to keep only the latest record per order while ranking delivery times within each region.
industryUseCases.solution: row_number over Window.partitionBy(order_id).orderBy(event_ts desc) for dedup, and rank over region-partitioned windows for performance ranking.
industryUseCases.benefits: Clean, deduplicated data and regional rankings in one job, avoiding error-prone group-and-join patterns.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Windows shuffle on the partitionBy key and sort within partitions; high-cardinality, low-skew keys scale well, while skewed keys create straggler tasks that AQE skew handling or salting can mitigate.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Window stages are ordinary shuffle/sort stages recovered via lineage; very large frames (e.g., unboundedPreceding to unboundedFollowing on huge partitions) raise memory pressure and can spill or OOM.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: No special HA needs beyond Spark's standard cluster resilience; window logic is stateless code shipped with the job.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Reprocessing from durable source data reproduces identical window results provided ranking orderBy clauses include deterministic tiebreakers.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Define a base window once and reuse it so Catalyst evaluates multiple functions in one window operator; pre-filter/pre-aggregate before windowing; prefer rowsBetween over rangeBetween for large frames when peer semantics are not needed.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Replacing O(n^2) self-joins with windows and combining functions over a shared spec reduces shuffle and CPU, lowering cluster-hours.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Standard data-access controls apply; ensure partition keys used for windowing do not leak sensitive groupings into outputs that downstream consumers should not see.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track the Window stage's shuffle read/write bytes and per-task duration; uneven task times signal partition-key skew.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Validate determinism by adding tiebreakers, check running totals for expected monotonicity, and confirm dedup reduces (never increases) row counts.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log partition-key cardinality and skew metrics; alert when a single partition's frame size or task duration dominates the stage.

recommendedPractices: **Always include partitionBy** on large data so work is distributed; omitting it funnels all rows into one partition.
**Add deterministic tiebreakers** to ranking orderBy clauses so row_number/first/last are reproducible.
**Specify frames explicitly** (rowsBetween/rangeBetween) instead of relying on the default to avoid surprises.
**Reuse a base Window spec** and derive frames from it for clarity and optimization.
engineeringStandards: Document the intended frame (running vs. sliding vs. whole-partition) for every window function in code.
Use rowsBetween for fixed-size physical windows and rangeBetween only when value-range/peer semantics are required.
Pre-aggregate or filter before windowing to limit the data that must be shuffled and sorted.
designRecommendations: Choose a partition key with good cardinality and low skew; consider salting for known-skewed keys.
Prefer dense_rank/rank/row_number deliberately based on tie semantics needed.
Avoid windows when a simple groupBy aggregation suffices, since groupBy is cheaper.
namingConventions: Name window variables by their scope and order (e.g., w_store_by_date, w_dedup).
Name derived columns by their meaning (running_total, moving_avg_7, day_rank).
documentationStandards: State each window's partitionBy, orderBy, and frame in comments.
Note whether ties are expected and how they are broken.
Document the default-frame behavior wherever the frame is omitted intentionally.
testingStrategies: Unit-test on small DataFrames with deliberate ties to verify rank vs. dense_rank vs. row_number behavior.
Test rowsBetween vs. rangeBetween on duplicate ordering values to confirm the intended frame.
Assert determinism by running twice and comparing outputs when tiebreakers are present.

commonMistakes.mistake: Omitting partitionBy on a large dataset.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Developers want a global running total or ranking and forget that no partitionBy means a single partition.
commonMistakes.impact: All rows are shuffled to one task, causing severe slowdowns or out-of-memory errors.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Always partition by a sensible key; for truly global rankings on big data, reconsider the approach or pre-aggregate first.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing rowsBetween with rangeBetween on tied ordering values.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The two look similar and both take boundary markers.
commonMistakes.impact: Incorrect aggregates: rangeBetween lumps all peers with equal ORDER BY values together, while rowsBetween counts physical positions, producing different sums.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use rowsBetween for fixed physical windows and rangeBetween only when you intend value-range/peer grouping; test on duplicate values.

commonMistakes.mistake: Relying on the default frame without realizing it changes with orderBy.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Users add orderBy expecting just a sort, not a frame change.
commonMistakes.impact: A sum 'over' the window becomes a running total (RANGE unboundedPreceding to currentRow with ties) instead of a per-partition total, giving unexpected numbers.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Specify the frame explicitly; for a whole-partition total use no orderBy or rowsBetween(unboundedPreceding, unboundedFollowing).

comparisonSection.explanation: A window function returns one row per input row with the group-relative value attached, preserving detail. groupBy collapses each group into a single aggregated row, losing row-level detail.

rowsBetween counts a fixed number of physical rows relative to the current row regardless of values. rangeBetween includes rows whose ORDER BY value lies within a range and groups all tied/peer rows together, so results differ when ordering values repeat.

comparisonSection.feature: Frame when orderBy is present vs. absent
comparisonSection.explanation: With orderBy and no frame, the default is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW (a running aggregate including ties). With no orderBy and no frame, the default is the entire partition (UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING), a per-partition aggregate.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between a window function and a groupBy aggregation?
beginnerQuestions.answer: groupBy collapses each group into one aggregated row, losing detail. A window function computes an aggregate (or ranking) over related rows but returns one row per input row, attaching the value to every detail row, so granularity is preserved.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: The core conceptual distinction interviewers expect: row preservation vs. collapsing.

beginnerQuestions.question: What are the three parts of a Window specification?
beginnerQuestions.answer: partitionBy (which rows form a group), orderBy (the ordering within each partition), and the frame (rowsBetween or rangeBetween defining which rows feed each calculation).
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Tests knowledge of the building blocks of Window.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between rowsBetween and rangeBetween?
intermediateQuestions.answer: rowsBetween defines a frame by physical row positions (e.g., 2 rows preceding to the current row). rangeBetween defines it by the ORDER BY value range relative to the current row and includes all rows tied at the current ordering value (peers). With duplicate ordering values they produce different results.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: A classic intermediate question; emphasize the tie/peer behavior of rangeBetween.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the default frame of a window, and how does orderBy affect it?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Without orderBy and without an explicit frame, the default frame is the entire partition (ROWS/RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING). With orderBy but no explicit frame, the default becomes RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW, i.e., a running aggregate that includes tied rows.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Frequently misunderstood; knowing this prevents the 'why is my sum a running total?' bug.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between row_number, rank, and dense_rank?
intermediateQuestions.answer: row_number assigns a unique sequential number even to ties (arbitrary order). rank gives tied rows the same rank but leaves gaps afterward (1,1,3). dense_rank gives tied rows the same rank with no gaps (1,1,2).
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Common ranking-function comparison; all require orderBy.

advancedQuestions.question: Why can omitting partitionBy be dangerous on large datasets, and what happens internally?
advancedQuestions.answer: Without partitionBy, all rows belong to a single window partition, so Spark shuffles the entire dataset onto one task to sort and frame it. This serializes the computation, often causing extreme slowness or out-of-memory failures. With partitionBy, rows are distributed across executors by key and processed in parallel.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tests understanding of the shuffle/single-partition mechanics behind windows.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you compute a true per-partition total versus a running total over the same data?
advancedQuestions.answer: For a running total, order by the sequence column and use rowsBetween(unboundedPreceding, currentRow) (or rely on the orderBy default). For a per-partition total, either omit orderBy (default frame becomes the whole partition) or explicitly use rowsBetween(unboundedPreceding, unboundedFollowing). The orderBy presence flips the default frame, so being explicit avoids mistakes.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Probes mastery of frame semantics and the default-frame trap.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: You must keep only the most recent record per (user_id, day) from a duplicated event stream. How do you do it with a window?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Partition by the dedup key (user_id, day), order by the recency column (event_ts) descending with a tiebreaker, assign row_number, and keep only rows where row_number == 1.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: w = Window.partitionBy('user_id','day').orderBy(F.col('event_ts').desc(), F.col('id').desc()); df.withColumn('rn', F.row_number().over(w)).filter('rn = 1'). The tiebreaker ensures deterministic deduplication.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a daily analytics pipeline producing running totals, 7-day moving averages, and top-N rankings per store over billions of sales rows.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Define reusable Window specs partitioned by store and ordered by date; compute running totals with rowsBetween(unbounded, current), moving averages with rowsBetween(-6, current), and rankings with rank over an amount-ordered window; deduplicate with row_number.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Windows avoid self-joins but require shuffles; high-skew stores create stragglers. rangeBetween gives correct peer semantics but can be costlier than rowsBetween for fixed windows.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Partition by store_id (good cardinality), enable AQE skew handling or salt hot stores, pre-filter to the needed date range, and reuse a single base window so multiple functions share one window operator.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: A Window spec (partitionBy + orderBy + frame) lets window functions compute group-relative values per row without collapsing rows like groupBy does.
keyConcepts: partitionBy = grouping; orderBy = ordering within group; frame = which rows count.
Window keeps one row per input; groupBy collapses to one row per group.
rowsBetween = physical offsets; rangeBetween = value range + ties.
Default frame: orderBy present => RANGE unboundedPreceding..currentRow; no orderBy => whole partition.
Boundaries: unboundedPreceding, currentRow, unboundedFollowing, numeric offsets.
interviewPoints: Window preserves rows; groupBy collapses them.
Default frame flips when orderBy is added.
No partitionBy = single partition = OOM risk.
row_number vs rank vs dense_rank tie behavior.
quickNotes: Add a tiebreaker to orderBy for deterministic row_number.
rangeBetween groups all peers (equal ORDER BY values) together; rowsBetween does not.
For a whole-partition total, omit orderBy or use rowsBetween(unbounded, unbounded).
Reuse a base window and derive frames so Catalyst shares one window operator.

keyTakeaways: A Window specification is built from partitionBy (grouping), orderBy (ordering within the group), and a frame (rowsBetween/rangeBetween), and window functions compute a value per row over that frame.
Window functions preserve every input row and attach a group-relative value, unlike groupBy which collapses each group into a single aggregated row.
rowsBetween counts physical rows by position while rangeBetween selects rows by ORDER BY value range and includes all tied peers, so they differ on duplicate ordering values.

The default frame is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW when orderBy is present (a running aggregate with ties) and the entire partition when orderBy is absent; specify frames explicitly to avoid surprises.
Always include partitionBy on large data to avoid funneling all rows into one partition, and add deterministic tiebreakers to ranking orderBy clauses for reproducible results.
